source.title: Weak-to-Strong Generalization beyond Accuracy: a Pilot Study in Safety, Toxicity, and Legal Reasoning
source.authors: Rui-Meng Ye; Yang Xiao; Bo Hui

record.file_problem: None apparent; the full paper text is present. Figure 1 is referenced, but its plotted values are not available in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: Applies weak-to-strong fine-tuning and reports PGR in new alignment tasks, including safety and toxicity. It also tests an ensemble-based training change.
record.gate_note: The paper reports safety and toxicity scores and PGR, plus qualitative text about legal reasoning. Table 3 contains example outputs, not a general performance measure; only its explicit statement that the weak and W2S models both fail on the unsafe prompt is recorded. No results from cited works are included.
record.test_reason: Fine-tunes GPT-2-medium on GPT-2-small labels (and GPT-1/GPT-2 for toxicity) and reports PGR in new alignment settings: safety classification, toxicity generation and legal QA. It also tests one training change, bootstrap ensembling of weak supervisors with voting. The setting is new relative to the original, so T3 fits better than T1.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right: the authors conclude W2S training beats weak supervisors in safety, toxicity and legal reasoning but stays below the ceiling, and that sampling/voting 'significantly improved' performance. Their own Table 1 contradicts that last claim. The raw score rises by 0.004 while PGR falls from 0.181 to 0.174, and the weak baseline also changes.
record.recipe_differences: Uses weak-model labels to fine-tune a stronger model and reports PGR, but applies this to safety, toxicity, and legal tasks rather than the original study's task setup. It also tests bootstrap sampling and voting over multiple weak supervisors.
record.method_sensitivity: In safety, sampling/voting changes the raw score and PGR in different directions: the score rises slightly while PGR falls.
record.peer_reviewed: Published at the ICLR 2025 Workshop on Bidirectional Human-AI Alignment (BiAlign)
record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported. The paper does not state evaluation sample sizes in the supplied text. Legal results are presented in a figure whose values are unavailable in the supplied text. Toxicity table results are not mapped to GPT-1 or GPT-2, despite both being mentioned as used.
record.rows_left_out: Table 3's other example outputs are omitted because the paper provides no ground-truth judgments for those examples; the unsafe-prompt failure is retained as an explicit textual result.

untested.parts: Auxiliary confidence loss and loss variants. Only ensembling with voting is tested, on safety only.
Untested as a whole: one model pair per task, and no size sweep or analysis of predictors. Task differences are confounded with model pair and metric.

missing.what: Numeric legal-reasoning results (balanced accuracy, F1, accuracy) for the weak, W2S and ceiling models
Which model (GPT-1 or GPT-2 size) is weak, W2S and strong in the toxicity experiment
Whether sampling/voting was applied to legal reasoning (the Discussion says yes) and its results

record.verdict_notes: Removed the record's V1 limits_scope: falling short of the ceiling is consistent with V1 (PGR>0), and the R16 anecdote is a single example. Removed V3 links and the V3 label: the study has no size variation and no predictor analysis. The toxicity PGR in Table 2 appears miscomputed (it is 1−PGR). This is a workshop pilot with no uncertainty estimates, no sample sizes for evaluation, and tiny models (GPT-2 small/medium).

versions.untested_parts: Tests the effect in safety, toxicity, and legal reasoning, but not across a broad set of models, tasks, or settings.
Tests sampling/voting with multiple weak supervisors in safety. Auxiliary confidence loss and alternative loss variants are not tested.

Reports results across safety, toxicity, and legal reasoning, but does not provide a clear model-by-model size comparison or predictors based on representations. Toxicity table entries are not mapped to GPT-1 versus GPT-2.
Does not test exploitable supervisor blind spots, distribution shift, or error similarity.
No theoretical conditions for beating a supervisor are tested.
